method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders' (January 2024), 28 claims; LICENCE: NIH author manuscript in PMC: "This file is available for text mining. It may also be used consistent with the principles of fair use under the copyright law." (© AGA Institute; not an open licence) (read at NCBI efetch JATS XML for PMC11163976 (Europe PMC fullTextXML returned HTTP 500), <license> element). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from British Society of Gastroenterology (Moran GW, Gordon M, Sinopolou V, et al.), Gut 74(Suppl 2):s1-s101, doi 10.1136/gutjnl-2024-334395 'British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on inflammatory bowel disease in adults: 2025 (Pouchitis section, GPS 55-58)' (first published 23 June 2025), 6 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC 4.0 (publisher open-access licence per doi.org/Unpaywall record); every PDF page footer also states: 'Protected by copyright, including for uses related to text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies.' (read at Unpaywall record for 10.1136/gutjnl-2024-334395 (publisher licence cc-by-nc) and the page footer of the University of East Anglia repository copy of the publisher PDF). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Europe PMC returned HTTP 500 for this author manuscript, so the JATS XML came from NCBI efetch (db=pmc&id=11163976); citation markers relabelled ref-type="ref" to "bibr" before pmc_text.py. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the pouchitis section of the BSG 2025 adult IBD guideline, read from the publisher PDF in the UEA open repository and converted with plain pdftotext (two-column). Its footer clause on text and data mining and AI training is recorded verbatim in the licence field; per the owner's standing decision such clauses do not exclude a source, so S2 is paraphrased and hash-anchored. No Australian pouchitis guideline was found (Europe PMC: pouchitis guideline/consensus 2020-2026). The ECCO Topical Review on Pouch Disorders (2025) was readable but is an expert topical review, all rights reserved, so the BSG guideline was preferred. S1's claims and anchors are unchanged. Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from S1 Table 3 (executive summary of recommendations), Table 4 (key overarching considerations) and Table 5 (definitions) added; S1 Tables 1 and 6-11 have merged cells and were not extracted. S2 is a PDF and has no appended tables.

claims.claim: **Pouchitis is the commonest complication after IPAA**, affecting 48% within the first 2 years and up to 80% at some point; about 17% develop chronic symptoms and 10% Crohn's-like disease of the pouch.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Normal pouch function** after the early adjustment period averages 4–8 stools a day and 1–2 at night. Pouchitis typically brings more frequent stools, urgency, lower abdominal cramps or pelvic discomfort; symptoms do not always match endoscopy or histology.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Chronic antibiotic-dependent pouchitis** responds to antibiotics but relapses within days to weeks of stopping. **Chronic antibiotic-refractory pouchitis** keeps relapsing or persists despite usual antibiotics and often needs escalation.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Crohn's-like disease of the pouch:** a perianal or other fistula arising at least 12 months after the last IPAA operation, a stricture of the pouch or pre-pouch ileum, or pre-pouch ileitis.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Intermittent pouchitis** means isolated, infrequent typical episodes that settle with treatment (usually antibiotics) or by themselves, with normal pouch function in between. The AGA set no episode count for antibiotic-dependent disease, because it is a spectrum running from 3–4 antibiotic courses a year to near-continuous use; pouchitis can also occur alongside Crohn's-like pouch disease.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Scope the pouch (pouchoscopy)** for frequent recurrences, poor response to antibiotics before other therapy, atypical symptoms, or suspected Crohn's-like disease. It is not routinely needed before antibiotics for typical, infrequent episodes.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Look for other causes when treatment fails:** anastomotic or stoma-site strictures and pelvic floor dysfunction impair emptying, and **C. difficile** and other infections should be checked in refractory pouchitis.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **BSG work-up for persistent symptoms after pouch surgery:** a pelvic MRI, stool culture and *C. difficile* test, and pouchoscopy that looks at the pouch, the pre-pouch ileum and the anal transition zone (rectal cuff). Faecal calprotectin and blood tests help grade severity; also consider pelvic sepsis, obstruction, stenoses and pelvic floor dysfunction.
claims.locator: British Society of Gastroenterology (Moran GW, Gordon M, Sinopolou V, et al.), Gut 74(Suppl 2):s1-s101, doi 10.1136/gutjnl-2024-334395, 'British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on inflammatory bowel disease in adults: 2025 (Pouchitis section, GPS 55-58)', first published 23 June 2025, https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/id/eprint/103386/1/BSG_Guidelines_2025_Gut_s1.full.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **The treatment goal is symptom resolution**; endoscopic remission was not treated as a critical outcome.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A pouch that looks inflamed but causes no symptoms may not need routine treatment** (AGA key considerations): healing on endoscopy or histology was not set as a target, for lack of evidence of added benefit. When looking for mechanical causes, strictures can sit at the ileo-anal anastomosis, the pouch inlet or the old stoma site, about 20–40 cm above the inlet.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No recommendation for or against probiotics to prevent a first episode** (evidence gap); **antibiotics are not suggested for primary prevention** (conditional, very low certainty).
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Treat infrequent episodes with antibiotics** (conditional). Ciprofloxacin and/or metronidazole are preferred, typically for 2–4 weeks; combine antibiotics if a single agent fails, and consider oral vancomycin when first-line drugs fail or are not tolerated.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Panel's standard regimen:** ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily, or metronidazole 500 mg two or three times daily, for 2 weeks; ciprofloxacin is usually better tolerated.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No recommendation on probiotics to treat an episode**; the panel's experience is that they have not worked well in practice and may delay effective antibiotics.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **BSG: first line for acute pouchitis is ciprofloxacin or metronidazole for 2 weeks** (ciprofloxacin is better tolerated and may work better). Warn about side effects and use the lowest dose for the shortest time that works.
claims.locator: British Society of Gastroenterology (Moran GW, Gordon M, Sinopolou V, et al.), Gut 74(Suppl 2):s1-s101, doi 10.1136/gutjnl-2024-334395, 'British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on inflammatory bowel disease in adults: 2025 (Pouchitis section, GPS 55-58)', first published 23 June 2025, https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/id/eprint/103386/1/BSG_Guidelines_2025_Gut_s1.full.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Doses from the BSG evidence:** ciprofloxacin 1 g/day and metronidazole 20 mg/kg/day both brought remission at 2 weeks in a small trial (7/7 vs 6/9); extend to 2–4 weeks if 2 weeks is not enough. A nightly budesonide enema (2 mg in 100 ml) matched metronidazole 500 mg twice daily over 6 weeks. A third (33%) had side effects on metronidazole (vomiting, taste change, transient neuropathy) and none on ciprofloxacin.
claims.locator: British Society of Gastroenterology (Moran GW, Gordon M, Sinopolou V, et al.), Gut 74(Suppl 2):s1-s101, doi 10.1136/gutjnl-2024-334395, 'British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on inflammatory bowel disease in adults: 2025 (Pouchitis section, GPS 55-58)', first published 23 June 2025, https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/id/eprint/103386/1/BSG_Guidelines_2025_Gut_s1.full.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **After antibiotic-induced remission, probiotics (the De Simone multi-strain formulation used in trials) are suggested to prevent recurrence** (conditional, low certainty); trials showed 87% lower relapse over 12 months. Patients with infrequent recurrences may reasonably choose no preventive treatment.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Chronic antibiotics are suggested** (conditional, very low certainty), after pouchoscopy confirms inflammation and excludes other causes. To limit resistance use the lowest effective dose (for example ciprofloxacin 500 mg daily or 250 mg twice daily), with breaks of about one week a month, or rotate antibiotics every 1–2 weeks.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Advanced therapies the AGA names** for antibiotic-dependent, antibiotic-refractory and Crohn's-like pouch disease (summary table): vedolizumab, ustekinumab, risankizumab, the anti-TNF drugs infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab and certolizumab pegol, the S1P modulator ozanimod, and the JAK inhibitors tofacitinib and upadacitinib.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Long-term antibiotics carry harms**, including resistance, neuropathy with metronidazole and tendinopathy with ciprofloxacin.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Advanced immunosuppressive therapy is an alternative** (conditional, very low certainty), particularly when antibiotics are not tolerated or long-term antibiotic risk is a concern. Drugs approved for UC or Crohn's disease can be used; vedolizumab is the only one with EMA approval for pouchitis. Drugs used before colectomy may be reconsidered.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Advanced immunosuppressive therapy is suggested** (conditional; low certainty for vedolizumab, very low for others). In the EARNEST trial 32/51 on vedolizumab responded at week 14 against 17/51 on placebo; pooled cohort response across drug classes was about 50%, with no significant difference between drugs.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refractory pouchitis is one of the commonest causes of pouch failure**, so delayed or inadequate treatment has consequences. Some patients keep getting partial benefit from antibiotics alongside advanced therapy.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Corticosteroids are suggested for short-term control** (conditional, very low certainty): controlled ileal-release budesonide is preferred, for under 8–12 weeks, with a steroid-sparing plan. Steroids need not be tried before advanced therapy.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **AGA summary table on steroid length:** keep corticosteroids short, under 8 weeks, in antibiotic-refractory pouchitis as in Crohn's-like disease of the pouch, and plan steroid-sparing treatment for the long term.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Sulfasalazine** may help people with infrequent episodes, but whether it works in antibiotic-refractory pouchitis is not known (AGA summary table).
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **AGA summary-table grades that differ from its text:** probiotics to prevent recurrence after antibiotic remission, conditional, very low certainty; advanced therapy for antibiotic-dependent pouchitis, conditional, low certainty for vedolizumab and very low for the others; against mesalazine in antibiotic-refractory pouchitis, conditional, very low certainty; the two probiotic items with no recommendation (primary prevention, treating an episode) are rated very low certainty.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **BSG for chronic pouchitis:** combine antibiotics (for example ciprofloxacin with metronidazole, tinidazole or rifaximin), or use budesonide or beclometasone by mouth. If it still does not settle, reassess for other causes before moving to advanced therapy.
claims.locator: British Society of Gastroenterology (Moran GW, Gordon M, Sinopolou V, et al.), Gut 74(Suppl 2):s1-s101, doi 10.1136/gutjnl-2024-334395, 'British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on inflammatory bowel disease in adults: 2025 (Pouchitis section, GPS 55-58)', first published 23 June 2025, https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/id/eprint/103386/1/BSG_Guidelines_2025_Gut_s1.full.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **BSG: vedolizumab is the suggested first-line advanced therapy** for chronic refractory pouchitis. In EARNEST (102 patients, all given ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 4 weeks), clinical remission was 31% vs 10% at week 14 and 35% vs 18% at week 34; a small adalimumab trial showed no benefit. Pooled cohort response rates were 54% for anti-TNF, 72.3% ustekinumab, 52.0% vedolizumab and 30.9% tofacitinib, with wide uncertainty.
claims.locator: British Society of Gastroenterology (Moran GW, Gordon M, Sinopolou V, et al.), Gut 74(Suppl 2):s1-s101, doi 10.1136/gutjnl-2024-334395, 'British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on inflammatory bowel disease in adults: 2025 (Pouchitis section, GPS 55-58)', first published 23 June 2025, https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/id/eprint/103386/1/BSG_Guidelines_2025_Gut_s1.full.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Mesalazine is not suggested** for refractory pouchitis (evidence gap); it may delay more effective therapy.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Crohn's-like disease of the pouch:** corticosteroids (budesonide preferred) and advanced immunosuppressive therapy are both suggested (conditional, very low certainty), after pouchoscopy confirms the diagnosis.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Cuffitis:** use ulcerative colitis therapies such as topical 5-aminosalicylates or topical corticosteroids (conditional, very low certainty).
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refractory cuffitis:** begin with topical treatment; beyond that, advanced therapies approved for ulcerative colitis may be used. In Crohn's-like disease of the pouch some patients still need long-term antibiotics for coexisting pouchitis alongside advanced therapy (AGA summary table).
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Barnes EL, Agrawal M et al.), Gastroenterology 166(1):59–85, 'AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Pouchitis and Inflammatory Pouch Disorders', January 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11163976/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Primary sclerosing cholangitis raises pouch risk:** pouchitis in up to 64%, and chronic pouchitis in 68.1% vs 34.1% of matched patients without PSC, with more severe inflammation and pre-pouch ileitis. A pouch can still be offered after detailed counselling.
claims.locator: British Society of Gastroenterology (Moran GW, Gordon M, Sinopolou V, et al.), Gut 74(Suppl 2):s1-s101, doi 10.1136/gutjnl-2024-334395, 'British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on inflammatory bowel disease in adults: 2025 (Pouchitis section, GPS 55-58)', first published 23 June 2025, https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/id/eprint/103386/1/BSG_Guidelines_2025_Gut_s1.full.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-24
